## Before the bench {.center}

### One tap, every mode

A tap is broadband. One impulse excites every mode the structure has, and a
single four-second recording contains all of them.

No shaker. No swept excitation. No force transducer.

### The prediction you can test today

$$
\frac{f_2}{f_1} \approx 6.267, \qquad \frac{f_3}{f_1} \approx 17.548
$$

No length. No thickness. No modulus. No density.

These are pure numbers, and your measurement can falsify them **without anyone
measuring the beam** — which is fortunate, because this rig's dimensions are
not decided yet.

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will do

1. Clamp the beam and measure the **free length from the clamp face**.
2. Tap, with the accelerometer **removed**. Strain channel only.
3. Tap again with the accelerometer fitted. Both channels.
4. Three taps each, at least.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two ways to waste the session

**A double strike.** A bounced hammer puts a comb in the spectrum that looks
like structure. Check the time trace before the spectrum, every time.

**Unplugging the accelerometer instead of removing it.** Its mass is still on
the beam, so the "unloaded" run is loaded too and the ratio comes out at 1.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) and one of the analysis templates —
[Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "The measured frequency ratios are … against a prediction of 6.267 and
   17.548, and the departure is in the direction shear deformation predicts."
2. "The two damping estimators give … and …; the half-power one is biased high
   on a record this short, and here is why."
3. "Fitting the accelerometer lowered $f_1$ by … %, measured on a channel that
   adds no mass."
